transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-18 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (Redwood SE), Jordan Kim (Auriga CTO), Priya Desai (Auriga ML), Carlos Mendez (Auriga Infra), Lena Park (Auriga Product)

Summary (auto): early discovery focused on model selection and deployment (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private), context length needs, multilingual support, and tool/function-calling. Customer to share workload and schedule benchmarks. Redwood to send pricing and security docs.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Jordan, thanks for making time. quick intro — I'm Alex, AE on the account, Maya is our SE, Samir is also on for any infra questions.
[00:12] Jordan Kim: Hey Alex, thanks. yeah appreciate it. we wanted to understand how Redwood fits into our infra, and specifically around model selection. we run a multi-lingual assistant and some code generation features, plus some tool calls into our internal lookup APIs.
[00:25] Maya Patel: Great. can you share a bit about scale and requirements? like average convo length, tokens per request, and what you mean by tool calls?
[00:35] Priya Desai: Sure. average prompt is around 1,500 tokens but with retrieval augmented replies we regularly hit 6k to 10k context when you include retrieved docs. we need long context support for legal/contract summarization as well. multilingual is important — en, es, pt, fr, ko — and quality can't drop significantly on non-english. tool-calling is basically function calls to our internal services for account lookups, pricing, and a real-time quote tool. latency SLO is 300-500ms tail for interactive flows.
[01:05] Samir Rao: got it. so heavy context, multi-lingual, and function/tool calling. how are you currently hosting models?
[01:12] Carlos Mendez: right now a mix — some in-house on k8s with huggingface stuff, and we also call out to hosted APIs for higher-quality generation. cost is a big constraint, and infra ops overhead is a pain.
[01:25] Alex Chen: that makes sense. Redwood provides Hosted API for fast setup, Dedicated for reserved GPU pools if you want predictable throughput and lower unit costs, and Private (VPC/on-prem) for strict networking and compliance. usually the model choice and deployment mode go together.
[01:37] Lena Park: curious about the model options — we evaluate open models mostly, and also can consider closed models if necessary. what are tradeoffs between models for long context and multilingual?
[01:45] Maya Patel: good question. short version: some open models are optimized for long-context — either natively or via chunking/retrieval — while others shine for multilingual fluency. we also have quantized variants and different kernel paths on our runtime that change latency and cost. for example, for 8k-16k context we often recommend models with native long-context or windowed attention. for multilingual, some LLaMA-family or MPT variants are better, but it depends on the target languages.
[02:10] Jordan Kim: can you give concrete model names? we want to compare to what we currently call via OpenAI and via self-hosted.
[02:16] Maya Patel: Sure. open alternatives people look at: Mistral-distil variants for cost-performance, Llama 2 variants — though some require licensing checks — together with extended context versions like LLama2-13B-32k or specialized long-context models like LongChain-X (note: paraphrasing), also models from the open-weight community like MPT-30B-instruct (with long context patches). Redwood has performance profiles for each and pre-tested quantization settings.
[02:40] Priya Desai: how about quality in non-english? we saw Llama 2 drop for Korean and Portuguese on our evals.
[02:47] Maya Patel: yeah that's a common observation. some families are skewed to english. cohorts like Mistral and some community models have better multi-lingual coverage. we also recommend running an eval set — Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization + model combos per workload and flag regressions.
[02:59] Samir Rao: and function-calling? we need robust tool-calling with structured outputs. OpenAI's function-call paradigm is familiar to us. how does Redwood support that?
[03:08] Alex Chen: Redwood passes through streaming tokens and supports structured outputs and function/tool calling. the runtime supports reliably returning JSON-ish structured responses; we also have SDK primitives for function invocation and automatic routing to your tool endpoints. there can be differences depending on model — some models are better at adhering to strict schemas.
[03:23] Jordan Kim: network/security — if we go Dedicated or Private, what's the onboarding? do you support VPC peering, SSO, KMS?
[03:30] Maya Patel: yes. Dedicated is a managed GPU pool with private networking and optional VPC peering; Private gives you a private control plane with customer-managed networking or even on-prem. we support SAML/SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS/HSM integrations for encryption at rest. we'll send the SOC2 + ISO docs as part of the pack.
[03:45] Carlos Mendez: great. three more infra questions: can we run custom kernels or specialized quantization like 4-bit NF4? our current stack relies on some custom bits in the runtime.
[03:55] Maya Patel: we support common quantization like INT8 and NF4 variants depending on model and hardware. some custom kernel work is possible but we'd want to scope that in a POC. our compilation/kernal selector picks optimized kernels per model. sometimes the transcription or notes will say "kernel" spelled as "kernal" in some transcripts, sorry.
[04:16] Priya Desai: what's the cost delta between Hosted and Dedicated for large context workloads?
[04:22] Alex Chen: depends on usage pattern. Hosted is easiest to start but per-token unit cost can be higher. Dedicated reduces unit cost at commit levels — plus you get latency predictability. For long-context jobs, batching and KV caching become much more important; Redwood's prefix/KV caching can dramatically cut cost for repeated contexts. we'll share a TCO worksheet that models your 6k-10k context runs.
[04:45] Jordan Kim: sounds good. can we run a benchmark? we'd like to test latency and cost on our representative set — multilingual prompts + function-calls + long-context docs.
[04:53] Maya Patel: absolutely. typical approach: 1) get your prompt set and representative documents, 2) we run a Dedicated benchmark and Hosted run, 3) produce latency/cost/quality comparisons and recommended model+quantization profiles. we can also set up a private pilot if you need VPC constraints.
[05:08] Lena Park: timeline — we're targeting an initial pilot in Q2, production by Q3 if things look good.
[05:14] Alex Chen: good. next question: how much engineering effort to integrate the function-calling SDK?
[05:19] Samir Rao: our SDK is lightweight — server side client libs and a small shim for function registration. if you need custom routing to internal services behind a VPC, that's usually a couple weeks of infra work.
[05:30] Jordan Kim: any gotchas around data retention and logs? we need to ensure PII doesn't leak and we have audit logs for model outputs.
[05:37] Maya Patel: Redwood's Hosted option can be configured for no-logging/ephemeral mode; Dedicated and Private give you stronger controls and local audit logs. we also support field-level hashing and KMS for keys. we'll include the policy doc.
[05:50] Priya Desai: model licensing — you mentioned Llama2 has license caveats?
[05:54] Alex Chen: right — Llama 2 family has specific license terms for commercial products; we can help navigate licensing, and our legal team can coordinate if you pick a model that needs additional review. some customers prefer models with more permissive terms or enterprise-licensed variants.
[06:10] Jordan Kim: what about chained tools and memory? we want to maintain a short-term memory per user that persists across sessions, and also call tools during generation. latency budget is tight.
[06:20] Maya Patel: for memory you can use KV cache and external state stores. Redwood supports streaming inference and KV caching to keep hot context on GPU which helps latency. tool-calling can be synchronous or async — if you need sub-500ms tail, we usually recommend pre-fetching and caching where possible and keeping tool results compact.
[06:40] Priya Desai: earlier you mentioned quantization regressions. how do you validate quality after quant? we can't afford hallucinations.
[06:47] Maya Patel: Redwood Optimize ties into evals. we'll run a set of golden prompts and regression tests post-quantization and flag any deltas. for critical flows we recommend end-to-end evals including multilingual checks.
[06:58] Jordan Kim: curious about the runtime — is it possible to run mixed workloads on the same Dedicated pool? like some high-accuracy low-latency instances and some batch async jobs?
[07:07] Alex Chen: yes — Dedicated pools can be configured with different node types or tiers; you can route by policy. you can set autoscaling and burst capacity so batch workloads don't starve interactive flows.
[07:18] Carlos Mendez: networking again — do you support strict egress controls? our security team requires outbound whitelisting and dedicated NATs.
[07:24] Maya Patel: yes, Dedicated and Private support strict egress controls and whitelisting. for on-prem we'd follow your networking model.
[07:32] Jordan Kim: what about model updates and version pinning?
[07:36] Alex Chen: you can pin model versions and rollout policies; Redwood supports canary rollouts and automatic fallback to a compatible variant if a model fails. full audit trail in the console.
[07:46] Priya Desai: performance question — large context like 10k tokens, are you chunking or do you prefer models with sliding-window attention?
[07:55] Maya Patel: both strategies are used. native long-context models reduce the need to reconstruct context, but can be heavier. chunking+retrieval reduces compute but requires smart stitching. Redwood's runtime supports both and we can show tradeoffs in the benchmark.
[08:12] Jordan Kim: do you have any existing customers doing similar multilingual long-context + tool-calling?
[08:18] Alex Chen: yes — a couple of fintech and legal customers. we can anonymize case studies and share performance profiles.
[08:24] Lena Park: licensing again — if we pick an open model but then rely on Redwood optimizations, does that affect licensing?
[08:31] Maya Patel: typically optimizations and runtime don't change the base model license, but we'd review specifics. our legal has worked through common cases.
[08:40] Priya Desai: ok — on benchmarks, when you run them, do you use quantized weights in Dedicated or float baseline?
[08:46] Maya Patel: we run multiple passes: float baseline, INT8 or NF4 quant, and sometimes 4-bit/ggml-style schemes depending on hardware. we'll compare quality deltas.
[08:56] Jordan Kim: what about model interoperability? if we start on Hosted and later go Private, can we keep the same model versions and rollouts?
[09:02] Alex Chen: yes — that's one of our selling points: same API and config layer across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. migrating involves capacity planning but you keep model pins and rollout policies.
[09:12] (small cross-talk)
[09:18] Samir Rao: quick ops note — for very long contexts we sometimes recommend offloading embeddings + retrieval, and using lightweight synth models for final generation to save GPU.
[09:28] Jordan Kim: any concerns with streaming and function-calling for mobile clients? we want to provide progressive results.
[09:33] Maya Patel: streaming is supported; function-calls can be emitted as structured events. for mobile we usually recommend edge-friendly SDK flow and server-side enforcement of tool security.
[09:44] Priya Desai: final question: what are typical onboarding times for Dedicated vs Private?
[09:48] Alex Chen: Hosted you can be up in days. Dedicated typically 4-8 weeks depending on commit and networking. Private/VPC or on-prem varies — often 8-12 weeks with security review and provisioning.
[09:59] Jordan Kim: ok thanks, that's helpful. next steps — we'll pull together prompts and infra constraints and pick a date for the benchmark.
[10:06] Alex Chen: perfect. recap of action items: Alex will send pricing and TCO; Maya will schedule technical deep dive and benchmark; Priya will share sample prompts; Carlos will confirm network requirements. we'll attach SOC2/security docs.
[10:18] Jordan Kim: great, thanks everyone.
[10:20] (meeting closed)

Notes on transcript quality: some model and product names were auto-corrected or mis-transcribed (e.g., "K-V cash" instead of KV cache, "kernal" instead of kernel). There are occasional filler words and quick interruptions.
